situation:
You are the marketing manager at STARLING SHOE WORKS, a chain of fourteen shoe repair and shoe care shops and the largest in its region. The vice president (judge) has asked you to settle what the chain will advertise about repair turnaround when its first out-of-state shop opens next month.

The chain's new ticketing system tracks every job from drop-off to pickup, and two years of that data put the average resole at five days. The launch campaign was built around a five-day promise, because COBBLE LANE REPAIR, the established shop in that market, advertises a week and turnaround is the one claim customers compare.

The chain's cobblers say the average hides the jobs that matter. Worn welts and older soles run closer to ten days, and the new shop will open with two benches and no back stock of leather. Promising five days would leave the counter staff explaining missed dates in a market where the chain is unknown.

The vice president (judge) wants you to recommend what the campaign should tell customers, and what the chain should look at first. Advertising the longer window gives up the one claim that was to carry the launch. You will present to the vice president (judge), who will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you for your work after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the vice president (judge) of STARLING SHOE WORKS. Business background is the same as the situation above. The artwork for the launch campaign goes to print this week, and the ticketing data and the shop floor do not agree about what the chain can promise.

You want the marketing manager to recommend what the campaign should tell customers about turnaround, and to say what information the chain should look at before that claim goes to print.

During the presentation you are to ask the following questions of the participant:
judgeQuestions: If a date is missed, who deals with it?
Is that a fair place to put it?
